title: Mixture of Cache-Conditional Experts for Efficient Mobile Device Inference
authors_venue: Andrii Skliar, Ties van Rozendaal, Romain Lepert, Todor Boinovski, Mart van Baalen, Markus Nagel, Paul Whatmough, Babak Ehteshami Bejnordi (Contextual AI / Qualcomm AI Research). 'Published in TMLR, June 2025' on the PDF header; arXiv 2412.00099v2, 24 Jun 2025 (PDF read = v2; first pass cited v3).
setup: Training-free 'Cache-Prior' routing: logits z' = z + lambda * Delta_avg * m_t, where m_t is the bitmask of experts currently in the LRU cache and Delta_avg a running mean of the logit range; the biased logits only re-rank, the mixing weights use the original logits; optionally the top-J experts are always kept (Eq. 9, Fig. 3). Models (Table 1): Mixtral-8x7B (8 experts, top-2, 46.7B), Phi-3.5-MoE (16, top-2, 41.9B), DeepSeek-V2-Lite (64+2 shared, top 6+2, 15.9B), Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B (60+4 shared, top 4+4, 14.3B). Quality evaluation is simulation of the cache (Wikitext perplexity, MMLU 5-shot, GSM8K 8-shot) with cache = half of the experts (Appendix D adds one quarter). On-device (Sec. 4.5, App. C, F): llama.cpp on two Snapdragon / Android 14 phones, mlock on, batch 1; 12 GB phone with 2 GB reserved (10 GB usable), 4-bit Qwen1.5-MoE, cache 30 of 60 experts per layer; 16 GB phone, 8-bit Qwen, cache 45 of 60. Best LRU cache size found by sweep (Fig. 14: larger caches lose speed because the OS pages out KV/activations). 10 runs per box plot. Cache-prior applied only to decode (prefill unchanged). No absolute tok/s anywhere; every throughput is normalised to the best LRU = 1x.

numbers.what: Miss rate, original routing + LRU vs Cache-Prior lambda=0.5, Qwen1.5-MoE cache 30/60
Mean expert lifetime in cache (tokens), original vs Cache-Prior
numbers.ratio: 2.2x / 4.0x / 2.5x / 2.0x (text says '5-9x longer' for Qwen and DeepSeek: does not match its own table)

numbers.what: On-device relative throughput, best Cache-Prior vs best LRU (12 GB phone/4-bit and 16 GB phone/8-bit)
Throughput vs hit rate (lambda 0.1..0.9, 16 GB phone)
Quality: Wikitext perplexity increase at lambda=0.5

numbers.ratio: n/a; Fig. 5/6 y-axis spans are 0.6-1.0 points absolute across the Pareto front (e.g. Phi-3.5 0.776-0.786), so the '<0.1%' cannot be checked from the figures

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Up to 2x speedup over LRU on mobile
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 'over 2x' / '2x' vs best LRU (best cache size per phone); relative only
phones are 12 GB (limited to 10 GB usable by reserving 2 GB) and 16 GB; 4-bit on the first, 8-bit on the second
training-free (learned-delta variant in App. E is optional)

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Inference-time version of the same idea
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: it is lossy runtime re-ranking of the router, so quality is not preserved exactly

why: Matches: batch-1 decode, llama.cpp, storage (flash) behind a RAM expert cache, throughput linear in miss rate (so a serial, I/O-bound model like ours). Breaks: (1) cache is 1/2 of the experts (1/4 in App. D) of a 60-64 expert 14-16B model, not about 4% (20 of 512 experts per layer = 2 footprints at top-10) of a 125B 512-expert model; the paper never goes below 25%; (2) the method needs router logits at runtime and top-J protection; our simulation swaps picks with no logits (random, f of the non-repeating picks), which is a different and more aggressive perturbation than a logit-ranked bias; (3) it is lossy: only measured on 14-47B models with 4-64 experts; (4) baseline 1x is the best LRU, whose cache size was capped by phone memory pressure, which inflates the headline.
quality_loss: Wikitext perplexity +0.1% to +3%, MMLU and GSM8K below 0.1% according to the abstract (lambda around 0.5); Table 2 (appendix) gives only qualitative text samples. Granular models (Qwen, DeepSeek) tolerate swaps better than Mixtral; large lambda hurts ('transient bias toward the cache state').
ablation: Yes, partly: Max-Rank and Cumulative-Sum-Threshold routing baselines (App. B), cache size 1/2 vs 1/4 (Fig. 11, 15), running-average vs calibrated logit range (Fig. 16), learned delta (Fig. 17), Wikitext/MMLU/GSM8K Pareto fronts vs optimal-oracle eviction (Fig. 4-6, 10). It beats the oracle (Belady) bound with original routing, i.e. routing change, not eviction, is what helps. No ablation of cache size on device beyond Fig. 14 (LRU only).
limitations: Authors state: very large lambda causes over-reuse; results rely on mlock and device memory behaviour; MoE design (granularity, shared experts) matters; they say retraining/architectural choices are out of scope. Only one model on phones.
contradicts_our_findings: No contradiction. Consistency check: our stickiness simulation f=0.5 at 2 footprints gives miss 0.237 vs 0.451 (ratio 0.53), the same size as the paper's Mixtral 0.53 and Qwen 0.46. But our test row says 'no router logits needed': the published method does need logits and a protected top-J, so our f is an upper-bound style proxy, not a reproduction. The paper's near-linear throughput vs hit rate supports our serial (not overlapped) figure of 1.33x rather than the overlap 1.12x on a machine without I/O overlap.
first_pass_corrections: Date/version: PDF read is v2 (24 Jun 2025, TMLR header); first pass said v3.
First pass 'Qwen1.5 35%->16%, DS 28%->7%, Phi 22%->9%, Mixtral 40%->21%' verified (Fig. 9 table).
Text says experts stay '5-9x longer' for Qwen and DeepSeek, but its own table gives 2.2x and 4.0x (not in first pass).
'MMLU and GSM8K drops under 0.1%' is an abstract claim; figures do not allow checking it.

title: Not All Models Suit Expert Offloading: On Local Routing Consistency of Mixture-of-Expert Models
authors_venue: Jingcong Liang, Siyuan Wang, Miren Tian, Yitong Li, Duyu Tang, Zhongyu Wei (Fudan / USC / Huawei / Shanghai Innovation Institute). 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026' on the PDF; PDF read = arXiv 2505.16056v4 (28 Feb 2026; first pass read v3 and could not see the venue).
setup: Analysis paper, no system: two metrics. SRP = best F1 of a segment router that fixes an expert set per m-token segment; SCH = hit rate of an oracle segment cache (cache size = rho x number of active experts, evicts the expert used least in the next m tokens). 20 MoE LLMs (3B-57B incl. Mixtral-8x7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, OLMoE, Phi-3.5-MoE, Qwen1.5-MoE, Qwen2-57B-A14B, NLLB-MoE-54B, SwitchTransformers) plus pretrained 1.43B TOY models for ablations; corpus of mixed domains, 22,528 samples of 512 tokens. No hardware is given. The only systems experiment is App. F: a naive on-demand LRU implementation on the TOY models, throughput overhead vs full-GPU compared with SCH.

numbers.what: TOY baseline, hit rate relative to clairvoyant optimum (=100), rho=1
Correlation of SCH with realised LRU / LFU hit rate across models
Correlation of offloading overhead (naive LRU system, TOY) with SCH

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Local routing consistency is a model property
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: SRP ranges 19-78 across models, with shared experts and many-small-expert designs lowest

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: cache of about 2x the active expert count balances hit rate and efficiency
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: true for group-1 models (turning point in SCH near rho=2); groups 3-4 (DeepSeek, Qwen1.5, Switch, NLLB...) have no turning point and SCH grows nearly linearly with rho (Sec. 5.1). The statement is about an ORACLE cache, not realised throughput
rho counts per-layer cache entries / top-k, so rho=2 is 2 footprints in our terms; but the paper only says 2x is a knee for the most consistent models

why: It supports the operating point loosely (2 footprints is a knee for consistent models) and its TOY result that LRU reaches 0.67 of the clairvoyant optimum at rho=2 (Table 4) would put the optimum for our model near 0.82 given our measured LRU hit 0.549, which is inside the range of the paper's oracle SCH values at rho=2 (0.46-0.97, Table 8) (derived guess, not measured). Breaks: oracle cache with look-ahead over m tokens; 512-token texts; no throughput, no hardware, no 512-expert model (largest 128 experts/layer); the only throughput check (App. F) is a naive LRU on TOY models and shows a weak correlation, which the authors themselves say means the model should not be the sole decider.
quality_loss: Not applicable (lossless analysis). Notes that local routing consistency trades off against local load balance at training time (TOY NoLB SRP 56.4 vs OverLB 36.4, Table 2), i.e. any stickiness imposed by training/inference has a quality or balance cost.
ablation: TOY-model ablations of load balance, shared experts, expert combination space (Fig. 5, Table 2); domain vs vocabulary specialisation (Sec. 4, Fig. 15-18). Cache policy ablation only LRU vs LFU vs oracle (Table 4). No cache vs layout vs prefetch ablation.
limitations: SCH relies on an oracle; main text has no real throughput, only the App. F informal argument and a naive TOY implementation; authors say throughput depends on the implementation and other factors.
contradicts_our_findings: No. It is consistent with our LRU hit curve and with the claim that realised LRU is far below oracle. It cannot be used as evidence for or against a speed-up at 8-32 GB.
first_pass_corrections: Venue: ICLR 2026 is printed on v4; the catalog was right, first pass could not see it on v3.
First pass 'size inconsistency 54B vs 57B' is not an inconsistency: NLLB-MoE-54B and Qwen2-57B-A14B are two different models (App. table).
First pass 'hardware not given in the part I read': there is none in the whole paper.
First pass omitted that the rho=2 knee exists only for group-1 models, and that the throughput appendix finds only r about -0.3 (decode).
SRP numbers (19 to 78, Mixtral 49) and TOY Table 4 (90.55 / 67.04 / 70.87) verified.

the catalog text is cut off and no occurrence of Edge0 exists in the issue or its 24 comments; 'whole-layer' loading for prefill is a path of Edge0 (arXiv 2609.18063, Sec. executor paths), a different source

why: GPU slot cache over pinned host RAM, mostly batched or concurrent serving; only the prefill dedup idea overlaps with ours (and it is trivial: unique-expert loading). The anecdotal Apple-silicon evidence (LFU without ageing 1.4-2.3x worse than LRU, staging 0.94-0.95x, hit rate flat vs residency on a 256-expert model) is the closest to our regime (unified memory, SSD misses, batch 1) but is one user's measurement, unreviewed and with no controlled setup.

ablation: None controlled. Comments contain A/B tests by their authors (zero-copy vs fill path on GB10: 25.4/51.5/62.9 tok/s at C=1/4/8 vs 8.2/13.7/14.6; plain LRU +12-33% and plain LFU +7-39% more disk reads than LFRU on a 24k-call trace).
limitations: RFC lists: PR 1 not for latency-sensitive serving (sync H2D, enforce-eager), single GPU only, LFRU only, no bias tensors. Open questions on memory accounting.
contradicts_our_findings: Potentially: comment 12 (Apple M4, 256-expert model) reports miss rate nearly flat vs resident experts (62.5% to 64.7% from 38 to 72 per layer), while our LRU hit curve rises steeply (0.454 / 0.549 / 0.686 at 1.5 / 2 / 3 footprints). The model, routing entropy and the tuner-chosen cache sizes differ (the commenter says the model's routing is spread thin), so it is a flag, not a refutation. It supports our result that prediction/staging does not help when the bus is the bottleneck (0.94-0.95x).
first_pass_corrections: First pass said the catalog's '12K loads to 32 unique' did not appear; it appears verbatim in the issue body ('32 loads vs 12K sequential - 375x').
'Edge0 switches to whole-layer' is not in the issue at all; it comes from the Edge0 paper (2609.18063). The catalog row conflates two sources (and the CSV text is truncated).

First pass numbers (30 tok/s, 97-100%, LFU 1.4-2.3x worse, staging 0.94-0.95x, 83.6-99.1%, 6.9 GB/s, 7.2 s -> 0.29 s) verified; the three recall figures are at unknown cutoffs (mangled in the e-mail quote).

New: a 131B/6B-active top-8 model (same class as ours) on a 96 GB GPU gets 33.6 tok/s at c1 and 4.18x aggregate for 32x concurrency (expert union), and host gather (14.1 ms) dominates miss cost, not H2D (3.9 ms).

title: ExpertFlow: Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Inference via Predictive Expert Caching and Token Scheduling
authors_venue: Xin He, Shunkang Zhang, Kaijie Tang, Shaohuai Shi, Yuxin Wang, Zihao Zeng, Zhenheng Tang, Xiaowen Chu, Haiyan Yin, Ivor W. Tsang, Yew Soon Ong (A*STAR CFAR / HKUST / HIT-SZ / HKBU / NTU). arXiv 2410.17954v2, 2 Apr 2026; ACM DAC '26 (Long Beach, 26-29 Jul 2026), 7 pages.
setup: System: (1) routing path predictor (transformer, trained per dataset; in-domain and cross-domain), (2) token scheduler that regroups tokens with similar predicted paths, (3) expert cache engine (prefetch predicted experts, correct mispredictions at runtime). Models (Table 1): Switch-32/64/128 (top-1), Mixtral-8x7B (8, top-2), Qwen1.5-MoE (60, top-4), DeepSeek-MoE (64, top-6). Hardware: one NVIDIA A40 48 GB + Xeon Gold 6338. Datasets: Alpaca, WMT16, XSUM, AIME2024. Baselines: Cache-MoE (= Eliseev & Mazur per-layer LRU with CPU fallback on miss), SE-MoE and Pregated-MoE (Switch only). Settings are (cache size CS = 2..16 experts per layer, batch size BS = 4..32), i.e. batched, GPU, experts in host RAM.

numbers.value: up to 2.12x (2.21x on XSUM cross-domain at CS=4, BS=16)

numbers.what: Hit ratio Switch-32 CS=16, BS=4 (ExpertFlow vs LRU)

numbers.value: Switch-128 15.26 -> 1.03 GB; Qwen1.5 35.21 -> 6.52 GB; DeepSeek 31.35 -> 6.38 GB; Mixtral OOM in AIG, 15.99 GB with offloading

'outperforming LRU by up to 61.15%' is in the intro, but Fig. 10 gives at most +35.67 points (71.89 vs 36.22; text says '15-36% higher') and 1.98x relative; 61.15 cannot be reproduced from the data shown. The 91.96% and the 61% are not the same operating point (LRU there is 76.61%)
experts that run are the router's; but tokens are regrouped by a scheduler and the predictor is a separate trained model

why: GPU (A40), batch sizes 4-32, 8-128 experts per layer, a separate trained transformer predictor per dataset, caches of 2-16 experts per layer on tiny-expert-count models; the cache-hit result is on Switch-32 (top-1, encoder-decoder). Not a router-stickiness method, so it is not evidence for family #6. Predictor training cost and generalisation to a 512-expert top-10 model are untested.
quality_loss: None claimed (router unchanged); no quality table.
ablation: Hit ratio vs LRU only on Switch-32 (Fig. 10); token scheduler on Switch models only (Table 2: 1.03-1.17x). No ablation separating predictor accuracy from cache policy on Mixtral/Qwen/DeepSeek.
limitations: Memory saving is vs all-in-GPU; the baselines SE-MoE / Pregated-MoE run only on Switch; token scheduler benefit grows with expert count and is tiny on Switch-32; no stated limitations section.
contradicts_our_findings: No. It does not test temporal stickiness, and its largest hit-ratio gain is at large batch size where LRU collapses (BS=16, CS=8: 36%), which is a regime we do not have.
first_pass_corrections: First pass 'hit 91.96% vs LRU up to 61.15% lower' merges two things: 91.96% pairs with LRU 76.61% (+15.35 points); the 61.15% claim in the intro is not reproducible from Fig. 10 (max +35.67 points).
Throughput 1.99/2.12/1.94x, 10x vs SE-MoE on Switch-128 (9.99x), A40 + Xeon Gold 6338 verified. Batch sizes 4-32 and CS 2-16 were not in the first pass.
Memory: text gives 15.26 -> 1.03 GB (-93.25%); the 93.72% of the abstract is not derivable from the text.
Token scheduler Switch-64 ratio computed 1.158x (text rounds 1.15x).

title: Fast Inference of Mixture-of-Experts Language Models with Offloading
authors_venue: Artyom Eliseev, Denis Mazur (MIPT; Yandex School of Data Analysis; Yandex). arXiv 2312.17238v1, 28 Dec 2023 (technical report, 12 pages; no venue).
setup: Mixtral-8x7B(-Instruct). Per-layer LRU cache of k experts (k=2 on RTX 3060, k=4 elsewhere; 8 experts/layer, top-2) plus speculative loading (apply next layer's gate to the current hidden state). Mixed HQQ quantisation: shared attention 4-bit, experts 2- or 3-bit; embeddings, gates, norms stay 16-bit; the 2-bit scheme averages 2.6 bits/param with metadata. Hardware (Sec. 4.3): free-tier Colab T4 16 GB (PCIe3), RTX 3080 Mobile 16 GB (PCIe4) laptop, RTX 3060 12 GB (PCIe3) desktop, A100-80GB SXM (reference; also uses offloading), cloud T4 for 3-bit. Batch 1, OpenAssistant conversations, sampling. Expert offload tier = host RAM over PCIe; no SSD tier.

same, pre-loading on top of LRU
Table 2, 3-bit experts, full algorithm (A100 / 3080M / 3060 / T4 cloud)

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Mixtral-8x7B with 2-bit experts (about 2.6 bpw with metadata)
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: '2.6 bits per parameter' stated for the 2-bit HQQ scheme (group 16, scale group 128)
LRU cache k per layer; plus speculative loading, which the catalog omits
-3.85 points (FP16 attention) or -4.93 (4-bit attention, the chosen config); no 'accuracy at equal RAM' comparison

why: Origin of '2-bit experts + LRU'. But the cache tier is GPU VRAM over PCIe host RAM, k is 2 or 4 of only 8 big experts per layer (k=4 is half of the experts, 2 footprints of top-2), the baseline is naive offloading not a bigger-cache 4-bit path at equal RAM, and the paper never isolates 'same RAM, fewer bits' (our byte-capacity simulation does). Their LRU-only gain (1.27-1.34x) is for a 25-50% cache, nothing like 4% of 512 experts.
quality_loss: MMLU 70.51 -> 65.58 (-4.93 points) for the chosen 4-bit attention + 2-bit experts; 2-bit attention is much worse (55.26). Perplexity: Wiki2 3.59 -> 4.61, C4 6.52 -> 7.42 (Table 1, 4-bit attn + 2-bit experts). Data-free HQQ, no calibration.
ablation: Yes (Table 2): naive offloading vs no LRU/no pre-load vs LRU only vs full, on four GPUs and two bit-widths. LRU is isolated (1.27-1.34x), prefetch is isolated (1.05-1.33x), quantisation is not isolated from offloading policy at equal memory.
limitations: Authors list: future work on further offloading strategies and speculative prediction; the 'not possible to prefetch next layer reliably without changing architecture' footnote. Mixtral only; no disk tier.
contradicts_our_findings: No. Consistent in direction: LRU helps a lot when the cache is a large share of experts; our simulation finds the 2.6 bpw gain at the same RAM is real only when the cache is small (8 GB 1.49x serial, 1.08x overlapped). Their Table 2 ratios are against naive layer offloading and cannot confirm or refute the equal-RAM comparison.
first_pass_corrections: All first-pass numbers (Table 2, Table 1 MMLU 70.51 / 66.66 / 65.58 / 61.83 / 55.26) verified against the raw text.
Missing in first pass: ablation ratios (LRU alone 1.27-1.34x, pre-loading 1.05-1.33x), the 3-bit column, and the odd naive 3-bit 3060 value 1.791 (higher than other naive entries, likely a typo).
Right-block labels: 61.83 and 55.26 belong to the 3-bit-attention and 2-bit-attention blocks with 2-bit experts; first pass wording was ambiguous.

title: HOBBIT: A Mixed Precision Expert Offloading System for Fast MoE Inference
authors_venue: Peng Tang, Jiacheng Liu, Xiaofeng Hou, Yifei Pu, Jing Wang, Pheng-Ann Heng, Chao Li, Minyi Guo (SJTU / CUHK). arXiv 2411.01433v2, 6 Nov 2024 (ACM-style 'Conference'17' template; no venue).
id_read: arXiv 2411.01433v2 (PDF, 15 pages; Fig. 14 also read as a rendered image)
setup: Built on llama.cpp (token-level dynamic expert loading, layer-level adaptive prefetching, sequence-level multidimensional cache with LRU+LFU+LHU priorities). On a cache miss, the expert's unimportance score s = f(gate) decides: high precision (importance high), low-precision copy (moderate), or skip. For Mixtral thresholds T1=0.6, T2=0.9 give 67% high precision, 30% low precision, 3% skipped (Sec. 3.2); top-1 always high precision. Models: Mixtral-8x7B (45B, 32 layers, 8 experts, top-2, 87 GB fp16) and Phi-MoE (42B, 16 experts, top-2). Hardware: RTX 4090 24 GB + 256 GB RAM + 64 cores + PCIe4 (float16 base, int4 replacement); Jetson AGX Orin 32 GB unified, model on Samsung 980 PRO NVMe (7 GB/s nominal, about 3 GB/s in practice) (int8 base, int2 replacement). Batch 1, 60 Alpaca prompts, in/out lengths 16 or 128 / 32 or 128. Baselines: llama.cpp (mmap), MoE-Infinity, MoE-Offloading (Eliseev&Mazur), Transformers, DeepSpeed, Fiddler.

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 9.93x is Phi-MoE on Jetson vs MoE-Infinity; vs llama.cpp it is 18.9x
only about 1.05x in decode, about -10% prefill

why: Closest hardware class (llama.cpp, batch 1, NVMe, unified memory). But: (1) low-precision copies are used only for misses; hot (cached) experts stay high precision, and extra storage for multiple precision copies is needed, so it is NOT 'store everything at 2.6 bpw'; (2) the huge ratios are against weak baselines: llama.cpp mmap page-faulting (about 0.07 tok/s) and MoE-Infinity (about 0.25-0.4 tok/s) on a 3 GB/s NVMe; absolute HOBBIT speed is only about 0.9 tok/s (Mixtral) / 4 tok/s (Phi-MoE) on the Orin; (3) 8-16 large experts per layer, 42-45B models; (4) 3% of experts are skipped entirely (not only quantised).
quality_loss: GSM8K -0.01 (Mixtral) and -0.01/0 (Phi-MoE); TruthfulQA within 0.02; the text says 'decreases by no more than 1%'. Two benchmarks only, only when 30% of loaded experts are replaced and 3% skipped, thresholds T1=0.6, T2=0.9 tuned per model.
ablation: Yes (Sec. 5.5): dynamic loading 1.19-1.57x (the part relevant to us), prefetch about 1.05x, cache policy 4.7-8.7% miss-penalty reduction vs LRU. Cache vs layout is not separated.
limitations: Stated: focus on GPU-centric computing; CPU helper mode gives smaller gains; Fiddler wins slightly on Mixtral (0.99x). Not stated: only two models, 2 benchmarks, weak baselines.
contradicts_our_findings: No. The ablation (dynamic loading 1.19-1.57x, biggest on the slowest link) is the same order as our byte-capacity result (8 GB: 1.35-1.72x serial, 1.08x overlapped) and shows the same dependence on link speed. The absolute numbers (about 0.9 tok/s Mixtral on Orin) confirm that NVMe-bound decode with 8-GB-class memory is far below our simulated 2-4 tok/s, but those are 87 GB-class fp16/int8 models, not 4-bit.
first_pass_corrections: First pass numbers (3.64x/9.93x vs MoE-Infinity, 13.0x/18.9x vs llama.cpp, Table 3 GSM8K) verified.

Missing in first pass: 3% of experts are skipped (T1=0.6, T2=0.9; 67/30/3 split), ablation 1.19-1.57x for dynamic loading alone, absolute speeds read from Fig. 14 (about 0.9 tok/s on Orin for Mixtral).
First pass 'Jetson Orin 32 GB unified, int8+int2, NVMe about 3 GB/s' verified.

title: MoE-SpeQ: Speculative Quantized Decoding with Proactive Expert Prefetching and Offloading for Mixture-of-Experts (v1); renamed Specter: Fast MoE Inference via Quantization-Enabled Multi-Step Speculative Offloading (v3)
authors_venue: Wenfeng Wang, Jiacheng Liu, Xiaofeng Hou, Xinfeng Xia, Peng Tang, Mingxuan Zhang, Chao Li, Minyi Guo (SJTU / HKUST). arXiv 2511.14102 v1 18 Nov 2025; v3 22 Oct 2026 (v3 code link is named specter_asplos; first pass said ASPLOS '27, I could not confirm the venue from the page text).
setup: A GPTQ INT4 copy of the target runs as the draft model on the GPU, predicts several future tokens and thereby the experts of future layers; experts are prefetched over PCIe while drafting (Expert Lookahead Buffer, three-phase prefetch, layer-aware cache); target verified in parallel (lossless speculative decoding). The offloaded experts stay FP16 ('official FP16 weights for the target and a GPTQ-quantized draft'); quantisation applies to the draft only. Models: Phi-3.5-MoE (42B, 16 experts, top-2, 78 GB), Qwen1.5-MoE (14.3B, 60+1, top-4), DeepSeekV2-Lite (15.7B, 64+shared, top-6). Hardware: one A100 40 GB (PCIe 4.0 x16), 24-core Xeon Silver 4310, 256 GB RAM. Baselines v1: Hugging Face Transformers, Mixtral-Offloading (same cache SC and same memory SM variants); v3 adds SpecMoEOff, vLLM, llama.cpp. Datasets C4, WikiText-2, HumanEval, GSM8K, GPQA; single request plus batch scaling to B=32.

numbers.baseline: Mixtral-Offloading-SC 536.7 ms; SM 351.8 ms; Transformers 960.5 ms
numbers.ratio: 3.29x vs SC; 2.16x vs SM; 5.89x vs Transformers
2.5x vs SC; 3.5x vs Transformers; DeepSeekV2-Lite 4.8x vs Transformers

numbers.what: Cache hit rate DeepSeekV2-Lite at 16/24/32 GB
numbers.baseline: LRU reactive (v1 Table 3: 29.2% at cache 6; 50.94% at cache 16; LRU with scaled cache 61.13% / 76.56%)

numbers.what: Expert demand vs speculation depth K, DeepSeekV2-Lite

numbers.value: 69.2 ms full; 83.5 w/o PIO; 94.4 w/o PIO+SIC; 130.4 w/o PIO+SIC+SEE

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Quantized draft predicts experts for prefetch
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: INT4 GPTQ draft; offloaded experts remain FP16
v1 abstract 'at most 2.34x'; v3 says average 1.50x, up to 1.88x vs SpecMoEOff (different baseline)
536.7 -> 163.1 ms = 3.29x vs Mixtral-Offloading-SC (not 2.34x: the v1 text gives both numbers against different baselines; first pass said it could not find 3.3x, it is in v1 Sec. 4.2)
baseline is Mixtral-Offloading (Eliseev and Mazur) re-implemented, then SpecMoEOff in v3

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: notes naive spec decoding can hurt MoE because of the expert union
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: v1 Sec. 2: 'naively applying speculative decoding to MoE models is often counterproductive'; v3 Sec. 2.3 'expert explosion', 6.0 -> 31.7 experts per layer

why: GPU (A100) + PCIe + FP16 offloaded experts + GPU-resident INT4 draft; the prediction is a draft model forward, which on CPU-only 125B-class decode would cost a full extra small-model pass. Does not support 'requantise the stored experts'. The union-of-experts finding (K=16 touches nearly half of the experts) supports our own union measurements against speculative decoding at 512 experts.
quality_loss: None for output (lossless verification); the draft's INT4 only affects prediction accuracy. Table 6 (v3) shows TPOT degrades 1.06x/1.31x/1.34x when 25/50/75% of prefetch targets are wrong (prefetch accuracy 0.785/0.575/0.410).
ablation: Yes (v3 Table 5b and v1 Table 4): fused kernel (13.02 vs 8.88 tok/s w/o), async prefetch (-5%), PIO/SIC/SEE components. Cache-policy comparison LRU vs LRU-scaled vs single prefetch vs speculative (Table 3 v1 / Fig. 17 v3).
limitations: v3 notes the benefit depends on memory regime; dataset diversity; v1 states that Mixtral-Offloading was reproduced and extended to other models.
contradicts_our_findings: No. It agrees with our finding that speculation widens the expert union (our k=2 speculative read 1.34x more bytes per accepted token than k=1 on a 2.6 bpw 8 GB cache).
first_pass_corrections: First pass said the 3.3x / 536.7 -> 163.1 ms figure was not found in the text it read: it is in v1 (Sec. 4.2): 3.29x vs Mixtral-Offloading-SC (2.16x vs SM, 5.89x vs Transformers).
First pass said the 'naive spec decoding can hurt MoE' note was not verified: it is explicit in v1 Sec. 2 and v3 Sec. 2.3 (6.0 -> 31.7 experts per layer at K=16).
First pass v3 numbers verified (163.3 vs 292.1 ms; 1.50x avg / 1.88x max); the 1.88x maximum is the Qwen1.5-MoE ratio (66.4/35.3), Phi is 1.79x.
Hardware details added: A100 40 GB, Xeon Silver 4310 24-core, 256 GB, PCIe 4.0 x16.

title: Making Every Verified Token Count: Adaptive Verification for MoE Speculative Decoding (EVICT)
authors_venue: Lehan Pan, Ziyang Tao, Xiao Wang, Zhimeng Zhao, Meng Wang, Yanyong Zhang (USTC; Tianyijiaotong Technology). arXiv 2605.00342v2, 5 Sep 2026.
setup: Training-free, lossless truncation of the EAGLE-3 draft tree before target verification: prefix chosen by maximising estimated accepted tokens divided by profiled verification cost C(k), with C(k) reflecting the growth of the activated-expert union. Targets: Qwen3-30B-A3B (main), Qwen3-235B-A22B (TP=8), Ling-flash-2.0 (TP=4), dense Hunyuan-7B; baselines vanilla AR, Lookahead, EAGLE-3, DDD. SGLang with CUDA graphs on A100 SXM4 80GB; draft tree steps=4, topk=8, 32 draft tokens; six benchmarks, T=0 and T=1; batch 1 main, vLLM batch 4-64 in App. C.5. No offloading at all.

numbers.ratio: 1.24x / 1.27x (the text's '1.23-1.27x' is for these high-acceptance benchmarks only)

numbers.what: Verified tokens / activated experts / verification latency vs EAGLE-3
numbers.where: Fig. 5, Sec. 4.3 (these are EVICT's own numbers, not quoted from another paper)

numbers.what: Qwen3-30B-A3B activated experts vs tree size
numbers.value: grows with tree size 4 -> 32; figure axis labelled 'Total Experts = 64'

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Verification cost grows with the union of experts
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Fig. 1: more experts and higher latency with larger trees; target verification dominates latency (Fig. 2)
-32.5% activated experts, -26.6% verification latency (Fig. 5)
EVICT has nothing to do with expert precision; it belongs with the speculative-decoding families (#4/#5)

why: In-GPU serving on A100s with no offloading; reduces verification token count, not bytes read from a slow tier. Useful only as a data point that tree pruning shrinks the expert union far less than the token count (-74.7% tokens vs -32.5% experts), which is the same reason our speculative variants read more bytes.
quality_loss: Lossless (verification unchanged); lower mean accepted tokens than EAGLE-3 in Table 2 by design.
ablation: Yes: eager vs CUDA-graph integration (EVICT slightly underperforms EAGLE-3 in eager mode because of CPU overhead), tree/threshold ablations (Sec. 4.4), dense-model check (Table 9: +2.6-11.3% on Hunyuan-7B).
limitations: Stated: depends on cost/benefit estimates and may be hurt by domain shift; benefit at large batch is workload dependent (HumanEval at high batch comparable to the untruncated backbone).
first_pass_corrections: First pass '1.23-1.27x over EAGLE-3 on Qwen3-30B-A3B across temperatures' is the figure for high-acceptance benchmarks (GSM8K, HumanEval) only; the six-benchmark average is 1.15x at both temperatures (202.82/176.34 and 195.17/170.11).
First pass attributed '74.7% fewer verified tokens, 32.5% fewer activated experts' to another paper (AcceptMoE); both numbers (and 26.6% lower verification latency) are in EVICT itself (Fig. 5).
Abstract: 2.35x max and 1.21x average (mean of 1.15, 1.22, 1.25 on the three MoE backbones) verified. Hardware: A100 SXM4 80 GB, TP=4/8 for the big models.

title: Bandwidth-Efficient Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts via Low-Rank Compensation
authors_venue: Zhenyu Liu, Yunzhen Liu, Zehao Fan, Garrett Gagnon, Yayue Hou, Nan Wu, Yangwook Kang, Liu Liu (RPI / UMass Amherst / GWU / Samsung Semiconductor). arXiv 2512.17073v1, 18 Dec 2025 (8 pages).
id_read: arXiv 2512.17073v1 (PDF; Fig. 6-8 read as text and one page image)
setup: Experts stored low-bit (INT2/INT3, GPTQ/HQQ-style) in host RAM; per-expert low-rank compensators (rank budget average 32 for Mixtral, 64 for DeepSeek; kurtosis-guided rank allocation) precomputed offline; at inference only the router's Top-n experts (n=1 for Mixtral, 3 for DeepSeek-MoE) get their compensator transferred and added. Models: Mixtral-8x7B, Mixtral-8x22B, DeepSeek-MoE-16B (64 experts, top-6 + 2 shared). Hardware: GPU-only = H100 PCIe 80 GB + DDR host memory (experts loaded on demand); GPU-NDP = H100 plus a SIMULATED near-data-processing device (512 GB/s, 512 GB) modelled with Ramulator following MoNDE. Input 256, output 128/256/512. Baselines: GPTQ, HQQ (accuracy); Mixtral-Offloading, HOBBIT (GPU-only speed); MoNDE (GPU-NDP speed).

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Low-rank compensation to keep the savings of 2-3 bit offloaded experts
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: this is the method; but 'keeps savings' holds only with a compensator transfer of 0.75-6% of an expert and only for Top-n experts per token

why: Speed: H100 + DDR over PCIe (2.37 tok/s baseline) plus simulated NDP; no CPU-only, no NVMe. As evidence about quality: plain 2-bit loses a great deal (GPTQ INT2 collapses, HQQ INT2 MMLU 37), the compensation recovers only part (Mixtral MMLU 47.5 vs 70.4), and on the fine-grained 64-expert DeepSeek-MoE model 2-bit stays near chance on MMLU (28.75 vs 45.03). That model type is the closer analogue of a 512-expert top-10 model. It also requires an offline compensator per expert (extra storage) and a router-guided runtime restore; DeepSeek needs a larger rank/more experts.
quality_loss: See numbers: INT2 + compensation, Mixtral-8x7B average -15.5 points, MMLU -22.9; DeepSeek-MoE-16B average -8.8, MMLU -16.3. INT3 + compensation is close to lossless on average (-1.1 Mixtral, -0.8 DeepSeek). Perplexity ablation WikiText 6.32 (rank 32) to 3.77 (rank 128) on Mixtral.
ablation: Yes (Sec. 4.4): number/position of restored experts (Top-1 vs Top-2; Top-3 for DeepSeek), rank budget 16-128 vs overhead, kurtosis-guided vs uniform rank (7.05 vs 7.55 ppl at rank 16; 3.77 vs 8.54 at rank 128).
limitations: Not stated as a section; the text concedes DeepSeek-MoE gains are small and may need larger rank or more experts; compensation settings are hand-configured per model family; NDP results are simulated.
contradicts_our_findings: No contradiction; it supports our flag that 2-bit quality for the 125B-class 512-expert model is unmeasured and likely severe (our OLMoE Q2_K perplexity +26% fits this direction).
first_pass_corrections: All first-pass speed ratios verified (5.17x/7.64x, 3.77-5.48x vs HOBBIT, 5.18x/7.63x for 8x22B, 2.95-5.93x DeepSeek).

First pass accuracy: 'uniform GPTQ INT2 collapses 70.03 -> 34.41' verified; added absolute INT2+compensation values: Mixtral MMLU 47.53 (-22.9 vs 70.38), DeepSeek MMLU 28.75 (near chance, -16.3 vs 45.03).
First pass 'vs HQQ +0.45% (INT3) and +8.24% (INT2) average, MMLU +1.11 / +10.50' verified; DeepSeek gains +1.63 / +2.30 verified.
